title: The Effect of Load and Volume Autoregulation on Muscular Strength and Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Hickmott LM, Chilibeck PD, Shaw KA, Butcher SJ
population: Resistance-trained individuals; 15 studies, 441 participants: 6 studies on load autoregulation (133 people; three used repetitions-in-reserve rated exertion and three velocity-based training, each against percentage-based prescription) and 9 on volume autoregulation (308 people; velocity-loss thresholds). Five of the six load studies were of men aged 17 to 28 with at least 2 years of training and one of teenage girls with at least 1 year. Not runners.
findings: Searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus and SPORTDiscus under PRISMA; the protocol was registered (PROSPERO CRD42021240506).

Autoregulated load prescription (repetitions-in-reserve based rating of perceived exertion, or velocity-based training) and standardised percentage-based prescription did not differ for 1RM strength (MD 2.07 kg, 95% CI -0.32 to 4.46, p = 0.09, SMD 0.21).

With sets and relative intensity equated, velocity-loss thresholds of 25% or less gave greater 1RM strength than thresholds above 25% (MD 2.32 kg, 95% CI 0.33-4.31, p = 0.02, SMD 0.23) and less hypertrophy (MD 0.61 cm2, p = 0.03).
The authors conclude that autoregulated and standardised load prescription produced similar improvements in strength.

In the load comparisons (133 participants, 247 comparisons; 6-12 weeks, 2-3 sessions a week, sets matched in all six), the three studies of repetitions-in-reserve rated exertion (Arede et al., Graham and Cleather, Helms et al.) gave MD 3.15 kg (95% CI -0.14 to 6.45, p = 0.06, SMD 0.30) in favour of autoregulation and the three velocity-based studies MD 0.88 kg (-2.59 to 4.34, SMD 0.10); the subgroups did not differ (p = 0.35).

The authors attribute the small advantage of subjective autoregulation to those groups training at a higher relative intensity (in about half of the exercises) and to longer interventions. Every included study had some risk of bias on RoB 2, and visual inspection of funnel plots showed no obvious publication bias.

The authors name subjectivity as the main limit of repetitions-in-reserve prescription: in one study of a squat set to failure at 70% of 1RM, calls of 5, 7 and 9 RPE came about 5, 4 and 2 repetitions before failure; they add that accuracy improves from set to set and closer to failure.
limitations: The meta-analysis of load autoregulation rests on six small studies (133 people), three of them with the RIR-based method, and the pooled effect is not significant; resistance-trained, mostly young men, not runners or novices. Comparisons are of prescription methods over 6-12 weeks on 1RM and muscle size, with no running, economy or injury outcome. Fixed-effect models were used, all studies had some risk of bias, and the autoregulated groups often trained at a higher intensity. Full text read 2026-10-31 (the supplementary tables were not read).
implications: The only synthesis in the corpus that compares ways of choosing the load: an effort-based (repetitions-in-reserve) prescription and a percentage-of-maximum prescription gave similar strength gains in trained lifters, with a small, non-significant advantage for the RIR-based studies that went with a higher training intensity. It supports an effort target as no worse than a percentage, not as better, and says nothing about double progression or about runners.
No evidence here on the novice or recreational lifter, who is the usual user of the strength page; the load-progression rule stays a default (grade D).
